newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-National Mutual NZ sees lower kiwi dlr.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-National Mutual NZ sees lower kiwi dlr.

text.p: The appreciating trend of the New Zealand dollar is well and truly over and the currency's Trade-Weighted Index will be down to 65.0 within a year, National Mutual Funds Management NZ (NMFM) said on Thursday.

In an interview with Reuters, chief investment officer Barry Lindsay said NMFM saw scope for a further easing in monetary conditions later this year. The rally in short term interest rates was running out of steam, and the easing was much more likely to come through the currency.
"We have an expectation...that the Trade-Weighted Index will decline to at least 65.0, looking out over the next 12 months.
"There should be a pick up in economic activity globally, and with a lower exchange rate New Zealand should be doing much better on the export front," Lindsay said.
The currency's Trade-Weighted Index has fallen to 66.3 from an eight and a half year high of 69.42 in early March.

Lindsay said forecasts for a rising current account deficit reinforced the view that the kiwi's upward trend was finished, but a more compelling reason for its recent weakness was the drop in the premium of NZ's nominal interest rates over the rest
of the world's.
Short rates have dropped to 7.15 percent from just over 10 percent in October.

Lindsay said the fall in rates was responsible for much of the sharemarket's rally over the June quarter. That market has gone from strength to strength, and Thursday saw the index of the top 40 New Zealand companies set a record closing high.
Lindsay said although NMFM believed interest rates had finished their dash lower, it had had maintained a moderately overweight position in New Zealand shares for the September quarter.

"We felt that while interest rates may well have come to the end of their rally, the next phase for the stockmarket would be investors becoming more confident that corporate earnings would improve in the next one to two years, and starting to price in that more optimistic outlook," he said.
Further gains would come from a rebound in the economy and a pick up in commodity prices.

"We think this next six months is going to be pretty flat for the economy...(but) we support the view that there will be gradual pick-up in activity over the next one and two years, with most of that strength occurring in the second year."
NMFM is part of Australian-listed National Mutual Holdings Ltd, which is in turn 51 percent owned by French insurer Axa-UAP.
NMFM had moderately reduced its exposure to New Zealand bonds to slightly above neutral from overweight, as it thought most of the gains in that market had already been made.
It was underweight in international bonds for the September quarter, and neutral on international shares.
Lindsay noted that listed New Zealand property shares had put in a very strong performance in recent months, which suggested the property market was set to strengthen further.
However, NMFM had moved to modestly underweight in listed property shares, from an overweight position in the June quarter.
"We have a feeling that they have run on too hard, notwithstanding that bright outlook for commercial property values over the next year or two," he said.
NMFM remains overweight in the physical property market.
